name: Crypto-exchange withdrawal-velocity governance
category: New — incident-response and blast-radius features at crypto exchanges
parent_research_topic: Beava use cases — current and potential applications of beava as a real-time feature server

domain_fit.domain_name: Centralized-crypto-exchange (CEX) withdrawal-velocity governance and post-credential-compromise blast-radius containment
domain_fit.one_line_definition: A CEX risk / security / treasury-ops team must, on every withdrawal request and every withdrawal-address-book mutation, score per-account per-coin volume, new-counterparty velocity, and burst patterns inside a few-millisecond budget so the request is routed to auto-approve, tiered manual approval, or hard freeze before the hot wallet drains.
domain_fit.representative_jobs_to_be_done: 1) Contain blast radius after credential / API-key / signer compromise — when an account suddenly attempts withdrawals to never-seen addresses or rapidly fans-out across many fresh counterparties, throttle or freeze within seconds, before the attacker (as seen in DMM / Bybit / WazirX / Indodax / CoinDCX 2024–2025 incidents) can drain the available hot-wallet allocation. 2) Enforce tiered approval governance — auto-approve small / well-known-counterparty withdrawals, route mid-tier withdrawals (e.g. EUR 50k–100k or N% of 30-day baseline) to a single approver, route large / atypical withdrawals to multi-signer quorum, and reject withdrawals that exceed per-coin per-day envelope or break a newly-whitelisted-address waiting period. 3) Compute and serve the per-account per-coin per-rail feature vector (rolling 1h / 24h / 7d / 30d count and sum; distinct-counterparty cardinality; days-since-address-first-seen; z-score vs. the user's own envelope and vs. peer-segment envelope; concentration ratio of recent volume to one counterparty) that the rules engine and ML scorer fetch for every withdrawal-API call. 4) Emit 'fire-when-counter-crosses-threshold' alerts and quarantine signals to SecOps / treasury so a human can pause withdrawals on a single account, a single coin, or a whole hot-wallet before the full envelope is consumed.
domain_fit.event_shapes: withdrawal_request (account_id, coin / asset / chain_id, amount, destination_address, withdrawal_method (on-chain | internal | fiat-off-ramp), source_ip, device_id, session_id, 2FA_method, api_key_id, requested_ts); withdrawal_address_added (account_id, address, chain, label, source_channel); withdrawal_executed / withdrawal_settled (tx_hash, on_chain_confirmed_ts); withdrawal_cancelled / rejected (reason); login_event (account_id, ip, device, geo, mfa_status, success); 2fa_change / password_change / api_key_created / api_key_permissions_changed / withdrawal_whitelist_lock_disabled; deposit_event (mirror of withdrawal — context for net-flow features); trade_event (used to detect deposit-then-rapid-withdraw cash-out patterns); risk_signal_inbound from Chainalysis KYT / TRM Labs / Elliptic on the destination address (category, risk_score, sanctions_hit). Key fields shared across events: account_id, coin, chain_id, amount_native, amount_usd, counterparty_address, device_id, ip, geo, ts.
domain_fit.feature_shapes: Multi-window sliding counters per (account_id), per (account_id, coin), per (account_id, chain_id), per (account_id, counterparty_address) pair: count(withdrawals, w in {1m, 5m, 1h, 24h, 7d, 30d}), sum(amount_usd, w), sum(amount_native, w). New-counterparty velocity: count(distinct counterparty_address, w) per (account_id, coin) — HLL acceptable for w >= 24h, exact for w <= 1h. Days-since-address-first-seen per (account_id, counterparty_address) and is_address_whitelist_locked flag. Burst / drain features: max(amount_usd) in last 5m, ratio(sum_5m / sum_24h), ratio(sum_24h / sum_30d_avg). Concentration: top-1-counterparty-share-of-amount in last 24h per account. Envelope / z-score features: t-digest / KLL quantile sketch of historical daily sum_usd per (account_id, coin) -> z-score of today's sum vs. user's own 30-day envelope; same against (segment_id, coin) peer envelope. Sensitive-event-since features: minutes_since_2fa_change, minutes_since_password_change, minutes_since_new_device_login, minutes_since_api_key_created. Cross-coin features: distinct_coins_withdrawn_in_24h, sum_usd_across_all_coins_24h. Hot-wallet-side aggregates: sum(amount_usd) leaving a given hot-wallet allocation per 1m / 5m / 1h (drain-pattern detection per Sardine / Voltage / Fireblocks). Windows are predominantly sliding 1m / 5m / 1h / 24h / 7d / 30d; tumbling calendar-day is used for the 'KYC-tier daily cap' enforcement that resets at UTC midnight (matches Coinbase / Binance / Bitget convention).
domain_fit.entity_grain: Many parallel grains, with (account_id, coin) and (account_id, counterparty_address) as the two highest-value ones. Typical keys: (account_id), (account_id, coin), (account_id, chain_id), (account_id, counterparty_address) pair, (account_id, device_id), (account_id, ip_subnet), (api_key_id), (hot_wallet_id), (hot_wallet_id, coin), (counterparty_address) (for cross-account counterparty heavy-hitters / mule clusters), (customer_segment_id, coin) (for peer envelope). The (account_id, counterparty_address) pair grain is the natural carrier of the 'has this user sent to this address before, and when first?' question that drives blast-radius decisions.
domain_fit.window_semantics_required: Predominantly sliding windows over short-to-medium horizons (1m, 5m, 1h, 24h, 7d, 30d) — the 1m / 5m windows are essential because the Bybit-class drain was 14,600 transactions in minutes. Tumbling calendar-day (UTC) windows are needed to enforce KYC-tier daily caps (Coinbase / Binance / Bitget all reset at UTC 00:00). Hopping windows (e.g. 30d hopping by 1d) feed the per-user behavioural envelope. Session windows (per login session) are useful for 'how much did this session withdraw before MFA-step-up was demanded?'. Approximate sketches: HLL for distinct-counterparty count over >=24h, t-digest / KLL for amount quantiles, CMS for heavy-hitter counterparty addresses. Exact counts are required for KYC-tier daily caps, per-coin daily caps, and the new-address 24h / 48h lock (Crypto.com 24h, Coinbase 48h after the initial 8h grace).
domain_fit.exactly_once_or_idempotency_needs: Strict idempotency required. A retried withdrawal_request must not double-increment the rolling-sum or the per-day cap counter, otherwise an attacker can force the engine to refuse legitimate retries (DoS) and a legitimate user can be falsely blocked. Idempotency keyed on (request_id / client_idempotency_key / tx_hash once on-chain). At-least-once delivery is the norm on inbound buses (Kafka, Kinesis, in-house tx-firehose).

technical_fit.latency_budget: Tight. Withdrawal-API call must complete in low hundreds of ms end-to-end (synchronous user experience); the risk-engine feature read is one component of that and should fit in low single-digit ms. Industry references: Fireblocks Policy Engine, AI-driven CEX risk-control systems claim 'response time at the millisecond level' (EORMC press release), Coinbase Real-Time Mode publishes 150 ms stateless / 250 ms stateful feature aggregation latency, Sardine and SEON quote sub-300 ms per decision. Beava's sub-ms TCP get / batch_get is well inside this budget and leaves headroom for 30–100 feature reads per withdrawal decision plus the rules / ML scoring stage.
technical_fit.feature_freshness_sla: Effectively zero. The just-arrived withdrawal_request must update its own per-account / per-coin counters before it is scored, otherwise a burst of N concurrent requests each sees the pre-burst state and slips under the threshold — this is the same atomic update-and-read invariant that beava's @bv.event / @bv.table model is designed for. Peer-envelope features and KYC-tier baselines can tolerate hours of staleness. KYT / TRM / Elliptic address-risk joins are externally-refreshed.
technical_fit.throughput_profile: Steady-state withdrawal-request EPS for a top-10 CEX is far lower than trade EPS (typically 10s–1000s of requests/sec, with bursts during volatile markets and during ATO-attack windows), but each withdrawal triggers many side-events (login, 2FA, KYT lookup, address-book-mutation) and many feature reads. Total event-bus EPS landing in the risk feature store for a top-10 CEX is plausibly in the tens-of-thousands to low-hundreds-of-thousands of EPS once login / trade / deposit context is included. Bybit-class drain windows generate sustained 5m bursts of withdrawal-requests (14,600 signed tx in a short window). Beava's published ~684k EPS on a single Apple-M4 core (TCP+msgpack, parallel=16) is comfortably above any single-tenant CEX steady-state and burst envelope. [uncertain] — per-exchange EPS for withdrawal-side traffic is not publicly disclosed.
technical_fit.read_to_write_ratio: Read-heavy. Each withdrawal_request writes one event but triggers 30–100+ feature reads (rules engine + ML scorer + manual-review dashboard re-fetch). Login / device / address-book events further amplify reads. Plausible ratio is 30–100x reads per write across the risk pipeline.
technical_fit.state_size_estimate: Bounded-to-moderate by AML-feature-store standards. A top-10 CEX has ~10–100M registered accounts (Coinbase ~100M+, Binance >250M users claimed but DAU much smaller). Per-(account, coin) grain across ~200 listed coins gives ~1B account-coin tuples worst case, but the hot working set is far smaller — only accounts active in the last 30–90 days, and only coins they actually hold. Realistic hot working set: 1–20M active accounts * (~5–30 KB / account for multi-window counters, address-book HLL, quantile sketch, recent-counterparty CMS) ~= 0.05–0.6 TB. (account, counterparty_address) pair grain is explosive but TTL-able (drop pairs after 90d of inactivity). For mid-tier exchanges (Bitstamp, Bitget, KuCoin) the hot working set comfortably fits one beefy node; for Binance / Coinbase it pushes single-node RAM and motivates sharding. [uncertain] — bytes/entity is an order-of-magnitude planning estimate.
technical_fit.cardinality_pattern: Mixed. Account cardinality is slowly-growing (bounded by KYC onboarding). Coin / asset cardinality is small and bounded (~100–500 listed). (account, coin) is bounded by account * listed-coin product but sparse. counterparty_address cardinality is explosive and unbounded (every external on-chain address ever seen, across many chains). (account, counterparty_address) pair grain is explosive in the aggregate, bounded per account in practice (users have O(10–100) regular destinations). hot_wallet_id cardinality is tiny (O(10–100) per exchange).
technical_fit.typical_state_lifecycle_and_ttl: Short-to-medium for live decisioning. Counter TTLs: 1m / 5m features age out fast; 24h / 7d / 30d windows need ~30–60 day TTL. Address-first-seen timestamps need 90d+ (Coinbase's 48h new-address hold plus a 30d 'is this a regular destination?' signal). User-envelope quantile sketches need 90–180d rolling. Sensitive-event timestamps (2fa_change, api_key_created) need to survive a few days. SAR / regulator retention is 5y but satisfied by archiving the upstream event log + decision log to cold storage; the live feature server only holds hot working state.
technical_fit.typical_feature_count_per_decision: 30–100+ per withdrawal decision. Counters across many windows and grains, plus device / login signals, plus address-book metadata, plus KYT / TRM / Elliptic address-risk join, plus historical-envelope features and z-scores. batch_get / pipelined reads are essential — this is exactly the workload beava's batch_get is built for.
technical_fit.durability_requirements: Crash-safe with audit reproducibility. Withdrawal decisions are not technically regulator-grade in the same way SAR-supporting documentation is, but they are audit-relevant (regulators, exchange security postmortems, victim civil suits all want 'what feature values triggered the freeze on this account at 14:32:07Z?'). Beava's WAL + periodic snapshot fits crash-safety; the exchange's core risk-decision log and event archive are the regulator-facing system of record. The 'refuse-on-network-FS' default is right for this audience. Gaps for production crypto-exchange deployment: no point-in-time / as-of read, no hot-standby (losing 30d behavioural envelope on crash even after WAL replay is operationally painful), no deterministic-replay-with-hash for audit.
technical_fit.deployment_topology_fit: Single-binary per region is workable for mid-tier exchanges (Bitstamp, Bitget, Gate, KuCoin, Bitfinex, OKX-mid-tier-deployment). Top-tier exchanges (Binance, Coinbase) need multi-region active-active for data-residency (EU MiCA / GDPR push EU-resident data on-EU), high-availability, and per-region rule-set differences. Beava v0 does not natively provide that. Sidecar-to-existing-risk-platform (Sardine, Sift, ComplyAdvantage, Hawk, Flagright) is the realistic adoption path — beava becomes the sub-ms feature substrate underneath the vendor's rules + case-management UI; that aligns with the 'Redis-for-stateful-features' positioning.

commercial_fit.who_buys: CEX risk / fraud / security-engineering teams; treasury-ops and hot-wallet-treasury teams who own per-coin envelope limits; MLRO / compliance-engineering teams (overlap with AML monitoring but distinct buyer); platform-security teams who own SecOps response to credential compromise; the embedded risk-platform vendors (Sardine, Sift, SEON, ComplyAdvantage, Hawk, Flagright, Unit21) and the MPC / custody platforms (Fireblocks, BitGo, Copper, Liminal, Cobo) who could embed beava as a feature substrate under their policy engine.
commercial_fit.market_size_signal: Large and sharply pulled by 2024–2025 incident losses. Chainalysis reports $2.2B stolen in crypto in 2024 and $3.4B in 2025, with the single Bybit Feb-2025 incident at $1.4–1.5B accounting for ~44% of 2025's annual total; DMM (~$305M, May 2024), WazirX (~$235M, Jul 2024), Indodax (~$22M, Sep 2024), CoinDCX (~$44M, Jul 2025), Nobitex (~$90M, Jun 2025) round out the postmortem set. North-Korean / Lazarus-attributed crypto theft was $2.02B in 2025 alone (+51% YoY). Binance discloses $10.5B blocked across 5.4M users in Q1-2025-to-Q1-2026 via 100+ ML models on its risk stack. The directly addressable risk-tech market across the named buyer list (Coinbase, Binance, Kraken, Bybit, Bitstamp, Crypto.com, OKX, Bitfinex, Gate, Bitget, KuCoin and the next 30 exchanges) is plausibly hundreds of millions of dollars per year in software + integration spend; the broader crypto-fraud-prevention vendor market is structurally pulled by every new headline hack. [uncertain] — there is no consolidated published TAM specifically for CEX withdrawal-velocity / blast-radius tooling.
commercial_fit.urgency_drivers: 1) 2024–2025 incident postmortems — DMM, ByBit, WazirX, Indodax, CoinDCX, Nobitex — are explicitly cited inside CEX security re-architectures; the Bybit $1.5B drain is a board-level event. 2) Trail of Bits Feb-2025 white paper 'Preventing Account Takeovers on Centralized Cryptocurrency Exchanges' became de-facto industry checklist. 3) Sift Q3-2024 index reports continuing rise in financial ATOs (808% YoY in 2023, further increase in 2024). 4) MiCA full applicability (CASP regime live 30 Dec 2024, transitional sunset through 2025–2026) requires fully-implemented transaction monitoring including withdrawal-side surveillance, and ESMA's 2025 guidelines explicitly highlight 'rapid exit after cash-out' as a red-flag pattern that on-chain + off-chain surveillance must catch. 5) EU Transfer of Funds Regulation imposes Travel-Rule obligations on every inter-CASP transfer with no minimum threshold from 30 Dec 2024. 6) FATF June-2025 update flagged persistent implementation gaps in the Travel Rule for VASPs. 7) Insurance carriers (Coincover, Evertas, Munich Re) underwriting CEXes increasingly require demonstrable real-time withdrawal-velocity controls. 8) Headline-driven user churn — Bybit lost ~$5B in net outflows in the week after the Feb-2025 hack — makes incident-prevention a CFO-level priority.
commercial_fit.regulatory_or_audit_constraints: Heavy and growing. EU: MiCA (Title V CASP regime, fully applicable from 30 Dec 2024 with national transitional periods to 1 Jul 2026), EU Transfer of Funds Regulation (Travel Rule, no de-minimis for inter-CASP transfers), AMLR/AMLA (applies 10 Jul 2027), AMLD6, GDPR. UK: FCA registration regime, MLR 2017, upcoming UK crypto regulation framework. US: BSA / FinCEN (CEXes are MSBs), OFAC sanctions screening, FinCEN SAR/CTR, NYDFS BitLicense (NY 23 NYCRR 200), state money-transmitter licensing patchwork, FBI/IC3 reporting. Asia-Pacific: Singapore MAS DPT-licence + PSN02 Notice, Hong Kong SFC VATP regime, Japan FSA / JVCEA (DMM regulatory aftermath, October 2024 onwards), South Korea FIU and VASP regime, Australia AUSTRAC. India: PMLA + IT Ministry 'VDA' reporting and CERT-In incident-report-within-6-hours rule (WazirX aftermath). Crypto-specific: FATF R.16 Travel Rule, CARF (OECD crypto-asset reporting framework, applies 2026). Data: GDPR / DPDP / CCPA / PIPEDA. Constraints push toward: (i) per-decision audit trail (who-asked-what-when), (ii) reproducible features at decision time, (iii) data-residency, (iv) right-to-erasure surface compatible with aggregate counters.
commercial_fit.time_to_value_signal: 1–2 weeks for a per-account per-coin velocity + new-counterparty-distance + drain-burst demo against synthetic withdrawal traffic. 1–3 months for a shadow-mode deployment alongside the exchange's existing rule engine, computing scores in parallel and flagging would-have-frozen events. 6–18 months for production cutover (model validation, MLRO sign-off where AML overlap exists, SOC2 / ISO 27001, runbook for WAL+snapshot recovery, MiCA technical-standards alignment).

competition.incumbents: Generic streaming / feature-store stacks underpinning CEX risk pipelines today: Apache Flink for stateful stream processing of multi-window velocity counters; Redis Enterprise / Redis Cluster as the dominant in-memory feature cache (also used by Coinbase / Binance-class workloads); Aerospike for sub-ms feature serving (publicly cited by PayPal, Barclays, Forter; analogous deployments in crypto risk); Apache Cassandra / ScyllaDB for historical event store; Tecton (Coinbase publicly uses Tecton + Real-Time Mode for sub-second stateful feature freshness in fraud), Feast, Hopsworks, Fennel, Chalk as ML feature stores. Coinbase has built its own rules + feature platform on top of streaming infrastructure (Real-Time Mode for sub-second stateful feature aggregation, AI-driven rules engine for sub-day response to new scam patterns). The dominant production pattern is 'Kafka + Flink + Redis-or-Aerospike + scoring engine + tiered approval / case management UI'.
competition.competitive_incumbent_per_domain: Fraud-vendor cluster (general-purpose, applied to crypto): Sardine (behavioural biometrics + device intel + on-chain risk; 200+ risk signals per transaction; explicit ATO + crypto-cashout focus; Visa partner), Sift (Money Movement product, claims to stop unauthorized deposits / transfers / withdrawals in real time), SEON (velocity + device + email-domain enrichment, explicit crypto module), ComplyAdvantage Mesh (50+ tracked fraud types including ATO, APP, synthetic identity), Hawk.AI (150 ms average response, 70% false-positive reduction), Flagright (no-code, sub-300ms screening), Unit21, Lucinity, Castle, Arkose Labs, SpyCloud. On-chain risk (deeper-end of the stack, complementary not competing on withdrawal-velocity per se): Chainalysis KYT / Reactor (~9 of top-10 CEXes), TRM Labs (100+ chains, sub-second API), Elliptic Holistic (2B+ labelled addresses, sub-second), Merkle Science (DMM postmortem), Crystal Intelligence (WazirX postmortem), Solidus Labs, Scorechain, Nominis. MPC custody + policy engine: Fireblocks Policy Engine (industry-standard tiered approval / transaction-rule DSL), BitGo, Copper, Liminal (WazirX custody-arrangement provider — itself the subject of the WazirX postmortem), Cobo, Coinsdo. Beava would slot underneath the fraud-vendor cluster as the sub-ms feature substrate, or under a custody platform's policy engine as the rolling-counter store; it does not replace KYT, the rules-authoring UI, the case-manager, or the MPC signing layer.
competition.beava_differentiator: 1) Single-binary, Apache-2.0, no broker / no ETL — every named buyer today stitches Kafka + Flink + Redis + custom code; beava collapses the velocity-counter layer into one process with declarative schema. 2) Declarative @bv.event / @bv.table primitives express withdrawal-velocity, new-counterparty distance, drain-burst, z-score-vs-envelope as schema rather than Flink jobs + Lua. 3) Atomic per-event update-and-read is the right semantics for 'this withdrawal_request must update its own (account, coin) sum_5m before being threshold-checked' — a class of bug that has bitten production Redis+Lua deployments in burst conditions. 4) ~684k EPS on a single core gives huge headroom over CEX steady-state withdrawal-side traffic and survives Bybit-class drain bursts. 5) HTTP/JSON + framed-TCP (JSON or msgpack) lets the existing risk-vendor rules engine, MPC policy engine, or in-house scorer call beava directly. 6) Apache-2.0 + no open-core matters to crypto buyers who explicitly reject mixed-licence dependencies for security-critical paths (especially after the 2025 supply-chain attacks). 7) WAL + snapshot + refuse-on-network-FS is the right default for a regulated buyer who otherwise would silently run on NFS and break crash recovery. 8) Sub-ms TCP get / batch_get fits inside the < 300 ms vendor SLAs published by Hawk / Flagright and leaves headroom for the rules / ML / on-chain-join stages.
competition.where_beava_loses_today: 1) No TLS — disqualifying for any CEX production deployment; even with an in-front mTLS-terminating proxy, security teams want mTLS to the feature store itself given the 2024–2025 attack surface. 2) No authn/authz / RBAC — every CEX needs per-tenant tokens, per-role access, per-team audit; especially for the risk-vendor multi-tenancy case. 3) No in-process sharding — caps single-tenant scale at one node; viable for mid-tier exchanges, painful for Coinbase / Binance scale where 100M+ accounts across 200+ coins exceed single-node RAM. 4) No hot-standby / synchronous replication — losing 30–90d behavioural envelope on a crash, even with WAL replay, is operationally unacceptable to a CEX risk team. 5) In-memory only — at top-tier-CEX scale, (account, counterparty_address) pair-grain spills RAM; tiered storage (RAM -> local NVMe) is needed. 6) No native point-in-time / as-of read — required for 'what was sum_24h for account X at the moment we froze it?' audit questions. 7) No native Chainalysis / TRM / Elliptic address-risk lookup hook — every competitor has this. 8) No trigger / 'fire-when-threshold-crossed' webhook — withdrawal-velocity governance fundamentally needs 'pause withdrawals when burst score > k' emitted by the feature server, not polled. 9) No multi-tenancy — risk-vendor adopters embedding beava across many CEX customers need either per-tenant binaries or a namespace + sharding story. 10) No native idempotency keys on push — required for at-least-once upstream buses so a retried withdrawal_request does not double-count the per-day cap. 11) No deterministic-replay-with-hash from WAL — audit reproducibility regulators ask for. 12) No native data-residency controls — EU MiCA / GDPR push 'EU data on EU RAM'. 13) No Kafka source / sink connector — every CEX has Kafka or Kinesis in front of the risk pipeline.
competition.integration_surface: Upstream producers: in-house withdrawal-orchestrator (HTTP/REST is dominant inside CEX backend), Kafka / Kinesis tx-firehose, in-process Python service handlers, MPC platform webhooks (Fireblocks / BitGo / Copper / Cobo events), KYT vendor push (Chainalysis KYT webhook, TRM Labs API, Elliptic Holistic). beava's HTTP/TCP-push model is well-fit for the in-house withdrawal-orchestrator pattern (the orchestrator already makes a synchronous risk-engine call before signing the on-chain tx) and unusual for the Kafka-only feature-store pattern (Tecton / Feast / Hopsworks / Fennel) — closing that gap would require a thin Kafka-to-beava-TCP sidecar or a native Kafka source connector. gRPC would close a recognised gap with Tecton / Chalk and matches what CEXes standardise on internally.
competition.scoring_engine_coupling: Both, plus a third stage. CEX withdrawal-governance stacks typically run (i) hard policy rules (Fireblocks-style DSL, FEEL, Drools, vendor DSL), (ii) ML scorer (XGBoost / LightGBM / sequence model on the feature vector — Coinbase explicitly ships boosted trees + sequence models + neural nets here), and (iii) tiered-approval workflow engine (auto / single-approver / quorum / freeze). Beava is feature-serving only; the buyer plugs it into all three stages, and the trigger/webhook gap is what blocks beava from also driving stage (iii) directly.

adoption_signals.existing_public_users_or_case_studies: No public beava case study at time of research. Comparable platforms with named public users for adjacent / overlapping use cases: Coinbase publicly uses Databricks + Tecton + Real-Time Mode for fraud and runs its own AI-driven rules engine; Binance publishes its 24+ AI security initiatives and 100+ ML models with $10.5B blocked across 5.4M users (Q1-2025–Q1-2026); Sardine is named in Visa partner directory and serves crypto on-ramps / off-ramps; Chainalysis KYT serves 9 of top-10 CEXes; TRM Labs and Elliptic serve major CEXes and regulators publicly; Fireblocks Policy Engine is used by hundreds of CEXes, custodians, and banks. Postmortem-driven case studies (DMM by Halborn / Merkle Science, Bybit by NCC Group / Sygnia / Wilson Center / Chainalysis / Halborn, WazirX by Crystal / Cobo / CloudSEK / QuillAudits, Indodax by Merkle / OneSafe / SlowMist, CoinDCX by The Block) consistently identify withdrawal-velocity / blast-radius controls as the missing or insufficient defense layer. [uncertain] — exact named CEX deployments of any specific real-time feature store product, with public throughput / state-size figures, are not independently verified.

adoption_signals.adversarial_pressure_level: Very high and fast-tempo. Crypto adversaries (DPRK / Lazarus, APT-class actors, well-funded criminal groups, malicious insiders, supply-chain attackers — see the 2025 Safe{Wallet} JavaScript injection vector) iterate within hours-to-days and have direct financial incentive to find every velocity-rule gap. Hot-wallet drains complete in minutes once a credential / signer is compromised (Bybit: 14,600 signed transactions in a tight burst). The combined headline-loss rate ($2.2B in 2024, $3.4B in 2025) makes this one of the most adversarial environments any real-time feature server will see — comparable to or above payments fraud, well above AML or analytics.

risk_and_non_goals.non_goals: 1) Full event archive / multi-year regulator-grade retention of raw withdrawal events — that belongs in S3 / Snowflake / BigQuery / Databricks Delta; beava holds derived features. 2) On-chain transaction labelling and graph-side mule-network discovery — owned by Chainalysis, TRM Labs, Elliptic, Merkle Science, Crystal Intelligence. 3) MPC signing, cold-wallet ceremony, hardware-security-module integration, signer-quorum enforcement — owned by Fireblocks, BitGo, Copper, Liminal, Cobo. 4) Case-management UI, alert-disposition workflow, SAR/CTR narrative generation — owned by Lucinity, Unit21, Sardine, Hawk, Flagright, Verafin. 5) Sanctions / PEP / adverse-media list maintenance — owned by ComplyAdvantage, Castellum.AI, Refinitiv, Dow Jones. 6) Device-fingerprinting and behavioural-biometrics primitives — owned by Sardine, SEON, Arkose Labs, BioCatch, Castle. 7) KYC / identity-verification — owned by Sumsub, Persona, Onfido, Jumio. 8) Model training, model registry, model validation — Vertex / SageMaker / Databricks / MLflow. 9) Withdrawal-orchestration / on-chain broadcast itself — that is the exchange's own backend or an MPC provider. 10) Long-horizon (>180d) behavioural baseline computation — Spark / Flink batch territory; the result lands in beava but is not computed inside beava.
risk_and_non_goals.open_engineering_gaps: To be production-grade for any CEX or risk-vendor adopter, beava would need (roughly decreasing priority): (1) TLS termination (mTLS preferred) — non-negotiable; (2) authn/authz with RBAC and per-tenant namespaces (OIDC / SAML / mTLS-cert-pinning for admin); (3) trigger / 'fire-when-counter-crosses-threshold' webhook surface — directly required for withdrawal-velocity-governance use case (pause-account-on-burst, route-to-quorum-on-z-score-spike, escalate-to-SecOps-on-distinct-counterparty-velocity); arguably the single highest-leverage feature for this domain; (4) per-read audit log (who-asked-what-when) — needed for incident postmortem and regulator audit; (5) point-in-time / as-of feature reads ('what was sum_24h for account X at the moment of the freeze?'); (6) hot-standby / synchronous-WAL replication so a node loss does not drop 30–90d behavioural envelope; (7) in-process sharding or a documented horizontal-scale story (consistent-hash router, replication, failover) — necessary at Binance / Coinbase scale; (8) idempotency tokens on push (dedupe by request_id / client_idempotency_key / tx_hash) — required for at-least-once upstream buses; (9) per-feature TTL and tiered storage (RAM -> NVMe) so (account, counterparty) pair-grain can survive past RAM; (10) gRPC surface in addition to HTTP/TCP; (11) Kafka source / sink connector so beava drops into the dominant Kafka-fronted pipeline without a sidecar; (12) deterministic replay from WAL with verifiable hashes (incident-postmortem and regulator audit); (13) multi-tenancy + namespace isolation so risk-vendor adopters can embed beava across many CEX customers; (14) native hook for on-chain address-risk join (Chainalysis KYT / TRM / Elliptic) so the rules engine sees an integrated feature view; (15) data-residency controls (EU-only RAM, US-only RAM, JP-only RAM — MiCA, JFSA, NYDFS); (16) right-to-erasure surface (delete-by-account-id) that does not corrupt aggregate counters; (17) Prometheus + OpenTelemetry exporters for feature-drift and burst-anomaly monitoring; (18) admin / governance API for runtime policy updates (raise the 5m burst threshold during a CEX-wide volatility event without redeploying).
risk_and_non_goals.trigger_action_required: Yes — strongly. Withdrawal-velocity governance is fundamentally event-driven ('freeze account when sum_5m > k', 'route to quorum when z-score > 4', 'pause hot-wallet when sum(hot_wallet_id) leaving in 1m > drain-pattern-threshold'). Beava today is feature-serving only, so the caller's rules engine has to poll and threshold. Adding a trigger / webhook surface — or a native 'fire when atomic counter crosses threshold' primitive on @bv.table — is the single highest-leverage feature add for this domain. Without it, beava can serve features but cannot drive the response loop directly, which means it slots in as a substrate under another vendor's policy engine rather than as a standalone product.
